metadata.title: Court of Treasons
metadata.seats: Either seat may be human or machine; the intended default is one human against one machine.
metadata.description: A duel of ambition, betrayal and deceit between two Houses. There is no board and no movement. Each House builds three public Standings, spends them as a per-turn Levy, binds Minor Lords with hidden Bonds of Servitude, and works quietly on the Revolution in the other House's lords. Promises are objects: they are recorded, they come due, and they are kept or broken before a Court that remembers. A House wins by taking the Throne, by buying it, by the Court's Favour, or by outlasting the other.
metadata.ancestry: Derived from Game of Treasons (design.xml, treasons-c). Board, movement, castles and sieges removed; four seats reduced to two; economy, promises, Minor Lords and the Court added.

digital_premise.rule: All hidden state is genuinely hidden. A House sees its own Bonds, its own hand, its own Ambitions, and nothing of another's except what has been revealed.
Trust is not a number a player is shown. It is derived, every time it is needed, from the Promise piles, which are public. Nothing else feeds it.
Simultaneous choices — votes, sides taken in a revolt, keep-or-break at the moment of truth — are collected and revealed together. No turn order advantage in a simultaneous decision.
Every random draw comes from a seeded stream. A game replays exactly from its seed.
The AI decides with only what the seat legitimately knows. A machine House that reads another's hidden Bond is a bug, and the invariant checker asserts it.

game.invention:
Game of Treasons had three stats that only ever accumulated. Cards added Military and nothing spent it; Capital starved in single figures; Gold was drained by the tax and by nothing else. There was no cost to anything, so there was no curve and no turn where the interesting question was what you could not yet afford.
Splitting each stat in two fixes all of it at once. Standing is what you are: permanent, public, slow to move. Levy is what you can spend this turn: refilled from Standing at the start of every turn, and gone at the end of it. Cards cost Levy. A few cards cost Standing, and those are the expensive, compounding, land-like plays.
This makes accumulation matter without letting it pile up uselessly, gives the game an opening, a middle and a late, and makes the Lord Paramount's tax bite, because the tax takes Standing.

stat.name: Military
stat.use: Combat, coercion, the cost of War cards

stat.name: Capital
stat.use: Votes, intrigue, the cost of Political cards

stat.name: Gold
stat.use: Bribes, dues, the cost of Intrigue cards

standing.rule: Standing is public and permanent. It changes only by cards that say permanently, by taxation, and by revolt.
Standing floor is 0 and ceiling is 15. A House at 0 Military cannot defend and is a target.
Total Power = Military + Capital + Gold, counted from Standing only. It decides the Lord Paramount and the Final King.

levy.rule: At the start of your turn your Levy is set to your Standing in each resource. It is not added to what is left; it is set.
Unspent Levy is lost at end of turn. There is no banking.
Costs are paid from Levy. A card you cannot pay for cannot be played.
Effects that say "spend" take Levy. Effects that say "permanently" take or give Standing.
Levy may be given away in a Promise's consideration; Standing may not.

tracker.name: Revolution
tracker.holder: Minor Lord, against the House that holds it

hidden_trackers.note: Unrest is three tracks and not one: a mutiny in the Military, the court turning in Capital, the guilds withholding in Gold. One track let the House suffering it choose where the loss fell, which is the wrong way round — the House causing it should choose.

deck_access.note: This replaces the board. In the parent game a die decided which deck you drew from. Here you choose, and the choice costs.

Seventeen decks worked on a table, where a deck is a pile you point at. On a screen every deck is a menu item, and one Draw action a turn meant reading nine options before acting. So the satellites were folded into the three decks whose resource already paid for them: access was priced in a resource from the start, and every other drawable deck was a satellite of one of the three.
deck_access.rule: Drawing from your own House deck is free and draws 1.
Drawing from a shared deck costs 1 Levy of that deck's resource and draws 1.
Paying 3 Levy of that deck's resource instead draws 2 and keeps 1.
Drawing from the World deck is free, but the card resolves immediately and is not held.
The Ambition deck may be drawn from only while you hold an uncompleted Ambition, and costs 2 Capital.
The Throne deck may be drawn from only by a Throneworthy House.
The Court deck is never drawn from. The Court turns it.
Hand limit 7, checked at end of turn, discarding your own choice.
deck_access.deck: Your own hundred. Always available, always free.
Military buys you a fight, and the cards that win one. Armies, coercion, and what is played inside a combat.
Capital buys you the Council, and the promises that decide it. Votes, oaths, legitimacy, and the Promises themselves.
Gold buys you lords, the levers that reach them, and the whispers that turn them. Bribes, poison, spies, Minor Lords, Levers and Instigators.
Resolves at once, on both of you. The reason a free draw is not free.
The road to being Throneworthy. In the menu only while you hold an unfinished one.
In the menu only while you are Throneworthy.

round_structure.phase: The Council sits and elects the Lord Paramount. Every revealed Minor Lord casts one vote for the House holding its Servitude; a lord whose Revolution has passed its Servitude abstains instead. The Court casts one. Ties go to the incumbent, then to the House with fewest Broken Words. Total Power no longer decides this: a title that accrues to whoever is ahead is a title that cannot be contested, and it was the worst-measured rule in the game.

The Lord Paramount takes 1 Levy of their choosing from the other House and gains 1 Gold Levy. The taxed House gains 1 Grievance. The tax takes Levy and not Standing: measured over three ranges of 300 seeds, a Standing tax gave a 14.6x win spread and handed whoever led first 54% of games, because the title fed the tax and the tax fed the title. Electing the title breaks half of that loop and taking Levy breaks the other half — the Paramountcy now buys a good turn rather than a permanent lead.
Each living House takes a turn in seat order.

Every Promise whose due condition was met this round is kept or broken now, both Houses deciding before either is shown. With two players this is the only phase in the game where neither House moves second, and that is the whole of why it is a phase.
Instigators resolve. A Minor Lord at Revolution 5 turns. Any resource at Unrest 5 revolts. Ambitions are checked. Throne challenges are answered.
If the round number is even, the World deck turns one card face up on the table.

turn_structure.action: Choose a deck and pay its access.
Play cards from hand, paying Levy.
Advance Servitude over one Minor Lord, if you hold a lever that reaches it.
Add hidden Revolution to a lord that is not yours, or 1 Unrest to a named resource of the other House.
Offer a Promise. Costs nothing to offer and nothing to refuse.
Open War, a Throne challenge, or the revealing of a Bond.

sequence.step: Standing becomes Levy and Unrest bites. Nothing is chosen.
Choose a deck and pay its access.
Play, Propose, Build Bond, Send Instigator, spend Grievance, buy Favour.
Open War, a Throne challenge, or the revealing of a Bond.
Play, Propose, spend Grievance, buy Favour.

game.invention:
In the parent game an Offer was a record inside the engine and trust was a number computed from it. That worked, and produced retaliation cascades nobody wrote. But a card game can do better than compute it, because a card game can put it on the table.
A Promise is a card. It names who owes what to whom and when it comes due. When it comes due the promiser chooses, in the open, to keep or break. Kept, it goes to the promisee's Word Kept pile. Broken, it goes face up to the promiser's Broken Word pile and stays there for the rest of the game.
Trust is then not a hidden score but a thing you can count from across the table, and — the part that makes it a game mechanic rather than flavour — other cards can read it. A card that says "target House with two or more Broken Words" is a card that punishes a reputation. This is the thing the genre does not have.
The pricing lesson from the parent game is carried over exactly, because it was learned the expensive way: a promise priced from where the promiser stands produces scrupulously honest liars, and a promise priced by what it would buy the promisee produces a game nobody can win, because a vote is always worth breaking at the moment it decides something. What closes it is consideration: having taken the payment, reneging must cost more than never having dealt. So consideration is part of the card, and breaking a paid promise is a public offence rather than a private one.

promises.rule: A Promise names a promiser, a promisee, a term, a due condition, and optionally a consideration paid at once.
Offering costs nothing. Refusing costs nothing. Nothing is enforced, ever: verbal only, and you may betray at any time.

An ALLIANCE is a Promise. There is no separate pact: PRM008 is named The Sworn Alliance and its term is Restraint. Everything an alliance wants is already here -- secrecy by default, a public variant, consideration paid up front, and betrayal at any time with nothing enforced.
promises.note: Decided 2026-09-20, converting the pool's 79 alliance cards. A card that FORMS an alliance is a Promise card and not an effect; only the cards that act on one -- voiding it, forcing it, barring a House from offering -- are effects.
promises.rule: Consideration is paid from Levy the moment the Promise is accepted, and it is not returned, whatever happens afterwards.
At Reckoning, a Promise whose due condition is met is resolved. The promiser chooses Keep or Break with everything they know at that moment.
Kept: the term is carried out and the card goes to the promisee's Word Kept pile.
Break: the term is not carried out and the card goes face up to the promiser's Broken Word pile.

Breaking a Promise that carried consideration costs 3 Favour with the Court rather than 2, and gives the promisee 1 Grievance either way. With two Houses there is no table for an offence to be against, so the Court is what stands in for one: it is the only party that still tells a paid betrayal from an unpaid one, and that distinction is the whole of what closes the pricing problem.
Breaking a Promise that carried no consideration costs 2 Favour and gives the promisee 1 Grievance.
A Promise that can no longer be kept because its term became impossible is discarded, not broken. The engine decides this, not the promiser.

Word Kept and Broken Word piles are public and permanent. With two Houses they are read by the Court as much as by the other House: Favour is where a reputation is paid for, and the piles are where it is recorded.
promises.term: I will direct my lords as you say.

term.name: Peace
term.due: End of the second round from now

promises.term: I will not attack you, nor instigate against you.
promises.note: Five of the seven terms this design began with assumed a third party or a crown. The ones below replace them, and they share a shape: at two players a promise worth making is a promise of forbearance rather than assistance — not to do a thing you plainly could.
promises.term: I will not commit against your challenge.
I will not buy Favour, nor instigate against your lords.
I will reveal one of my Ambitions, truthfully.
I will pay you a named Levy.
I will free one of my Minor Lords.
My lords will not vote at all.

trust.rule: Trust is per pair and derived only from piles: Promises kept to you, minus Promises broken against you.
A House that has never dealt with you is neither trusted nor distrusted. Zero is ignorance, not suspicion.
Reputation is the count of your Broken Words, read by any House and by any card that names it.
trust.ai_note: A machine House prices a Promise by what the term would buy the House being promised, adds any consideration already taken to the cost of breaking, and uses the same valuation function whether it is buying or selling. All three are required together; the parent game measured what happens when any one is missing.

game.invention:
Servitude needed somebody to bend the knee, and with one opponent the only available knee belonged to a player who can simply decline. So the knee belongs to a card.
A Minor Lord is played in front of a House and stays there. It is bound with Levers exactly as the design already described; it serves while its Servitude holds; and the other House works on its Revolution until it turns. Everything a Bond was — built over several turns, half hidden, biting when it matures — survives intact. What goes is only the assumption that the knee belonged to a player.
This is also the conversion the rest of the game was asking for. In a duel the thing you attack, bind, corrupt and lose has to sit on the table, because the other chair can always decline.
Of the 24 cards written against vassals, Lords, Servitude or Bonds, none die: sixteen work unchanged, because the design already treated a vassal as a subject rather than as an opponent.

minor_lords.rule: A Minor Lord is a card. It is played face up in front of a House and remains in play until it dies, turns, or is freed.
A lord carries one Trait: In Debt, Afraid, Ambitious, Proud, or Owed. Levers name a Trait, and a Lever reaches only a lord that carries it.

A lord does not fight. Military fights, Capital votes and Gold buys; a lord that both voted and fought would collapse two of those into one card. A few cards grant a lord to a combat as an exception, and it is written on those cards.
A revealed lord votes at every Council for the House holding its Servitude, and pays 1 Levy of that House's choosing each round.
Gold binds a lord, Capital is what a lord produces, and Military never touches one. Each resource keeps its own layer.
minor_lords.trait: Reachable by a Lever of debt. Pays 2 Levy of dues rather than 1.
Reachable by a Lever of fear. Its Revolution advances at half rate, rounded down.
Reachable by a Lever of favour or office. Casts 2 votes, and its Revolution advances at double rate.
Reachable by a Lever of marriage or honour. Cannot be bound below Servitude 2, and never abstains.
Reachable by a Lever of a kept Promise. Free to bind for the House it is owed by, and worthless to the other.

bonds.rule: A Bond exists between a House and a Minor Lord and carries two hidden counts: Servitude, held by the House, and Revolution, held by the lord.
At most one Bond per lord. A House may hold as many lords as it can bind.

servitude.rule: Advancing costs a turn action and a lever: a card of type Lever naming a Trait the lord carries.
At 5 the House may reveal the lord, which puts it on the Council.
A revealed lord votes as its House holds, pays 1 Levy of dues each round, and cannot be targeted by that House's own cards.
Goldwyn's lords cost double to maintain: 2 Levy of dues, not 1.

revolution.rule: Track 0 to 5, hidden from the House that holds the lord.
The other House advances it with Instigators. A lord advances it alone once per round only while unrevealed.
A House may spy on a lord it holds at a cost, learning the count, with a risk of detection that gives the lord 1 free Revolution if it fails.
Revolution against a lord held by Aldemar begins at -1, taken once when the Bond is sworn.

When Revolution passes Servitude, the lord abstains at Councils. This is how a hidden track resolves in public without ever printing the number: you learn a lord has turned by watching it not raise its hand.
revolution.type: The lord is freed and returns to its deck.
The lord is freed and joins the other House at Servitude 1.
The lord is freed, joins the other House at Servitude 2, and the House that held it loses 2 Capital Standing.
revolution.rule: Revolution resets to 0 when a lord turns. Servitude does not survive it; a lord must be bound again from 0.

target.type: A lord the other House holds

target.effect: +1 Revolution, recorded as a false flag

target.type: A named resource of the other House

instigators.rule: Instigators are sent face down and resolve at Consequence. The target learns the effect but not the sender, unless a card reveals it.
Ravenmark cannot send Instigators. Vipren sends two per turn.

unrest.rule: Unrest is three tracks, one per resource: a mutiny in the Military, the court turning in Capital, the guilds withholding in Gold. Each runs 0 to 5 and each is public.

At 1 to 4, that resource's Levy is reduced by that many. One track let the House suffering it spread the loss where it hurt least; three tracks let the House causing it choose where it hurts most, which is the difference between a tax and an attack.

At 5 that resource revolts at Consequence: lose 2 Standing in it, reset to 0. A revolt is no longer a vassal going free. It is a thing you own turning on you, which is what the word meant before there was a board.
Removal costs 2 Gold per point, or 1 Gold for Goldwyn, or by card, or by a military crackdown which clears 2 of one track and gives the other House 1 Grievance.
A Lever may be attached to a resource instead of a lord. While it holds, that resource's Unrest cannot be cleared.

grievance.note: In the parent game Grievance sat pinned at its maximum in every single game, because the design gave it five sinks and the engine built none of them. Here the sinks are built first, and a large number of cards take Grievance as part of their cost, so that it moves. The coalition sink is gone: there is no third House whose attack you could join.
grievance.rule: Max 10. Gained from taxation, from broken promises, from crackdowns, and from cards.

Grievance is held against the Lord Paramount and is spent freely. With two Houses the table is one House, so what it measures is not a grudge against a rival but a grudge against whoever is being taxed for.
grievance.spend: Cancel this round's tax against you.
Play one Rebellion card from any discard pile.
Attempt an assassination against the Lord Paramount.
Force a Council immediately, which re-elects the Lord Paramount.
grievance.rule: Many War and Political cards name Grievance in their cost. That is the intended main drain; the five sinks above are the floor, not the whole of it.

combat.rule: Combat is declared against one House. It needs Open War, or a card that permits it, or a Throne challenge.
Each side commits Military Levy secretly, then reveals. Each may then play one Combat card.
Higher committed total wins. Ravenmark wins ties; otherwise the defender wins ties.
Committed Levy is spent either way. The loser also loses 1 Military Standing.
The winner takes 1 Standing of their choice from the loser, or 1 Unrest into a resource of their choosing, or forces the discard of two cards.
A House reduced to 0 Military Standing cannot commit and automatically loses any combat it is forced into.
A combat may not take a House's last point of Standing. It may grind one to 1 and hold it there; it may not finish it.
combat.note: The floor was added 2026-09-20 because without it the game was decided at setup. The three clauses above compound: Ravenmark declares free every turn, each win takes Standing, and no card a low-Gold House can afford restores Military Standing -- the recovery cards cost either 4M, which a House at 0 Military cannot have, or 4G, above Vipren's Gold Standing of 3. Measured over three ranges of 300 seeds, Ravenmark beat Vipren 83-0 and Goldwyn 55-0 with no game in either, and every matchup was decided by the starting Military Standing and nothing that happened afterwards. Withholding the spoil entirely was tried first and inverted the game -- Ravenmark 68% to 3.5% -- because the Standing it takes IS its economy. Only the killing blow is withheld.
combat.rule: Declaring Open War costs 2 Grievance, except for Ravenmark, who declares free. Vipren cannot declare without paying 4.
Vipren pays double for Combat cards.

council.note: A Council of two Houses is an argument. A Council of the Minor Lords in play is a real one, and everything it needs is already on the table. This is what the lords are for, and it is why binding them is worth a turn.
council.trigger: Accession, every round. A Council card resolving, a World card, or 6 Grievance spent calls another.
council.rule: Every revealed Minor Lord casts one vote, for the House holding its Servitude. An Ambitious lord casts two.
A lord whose Revolution has passed its Servitude abstains. Neither House is told the counts; they are told who did not vote.
The Court casts one vote, for the House with the higher Favour, abstaining below +3.
Neither House votes. A House with no lords has no voice, which is the cost of never binding one.
A card that speaks of "your vote" therefore reaches your LORDS. A House whose vote counts twice has each of its revealed lords cast one more, and a House with none gains nothing from such a card.
A tie may be settled by a card. A duel ties constantly -- two Houses and a handful of lords -- so a card that decides one is worth more here than at a table of four.
council.note: Decided 2026-09-20, converting the pool's 73 voting cards. Most were written for a game where the players vote; here the lords do, so those cards are about the lords or they are about nothing. The procedural ones -- quorums, "vote requires 3+ players", coin flips -- are about nothing and are not converted.
council.rule: Aldemar's lords each cast one extra vote. Goldwyn may buy votes at 2 Gold Levy each, declared before the reveal.
Promises of type Vote or Abstention come due here, and bind how a House directs its lords.
council.decides: The Lord Paramount, who takes the tax. Nothing else, and nobody is crowned: winning by vote is not a road in this game.
council.rule: On a tie the incumbent holds. If neither House holds it, neither takes the tax that round.

ambitions.note: This replaces the twelve-space inner gauntlet. The goals were already cards in the parent design; only the track needed removing.
ambitions.rule: At setup each House is dealt 6 Ambitions, face down, known only to itself. The Disclosure promise is the only way one House learns another's, and it is the only promise whose keeping is checkable on the spot.
Completing 3 makes a House Throneworthy. An Ambition is revealed when completed, and completion is checked at Consequence.
A completed Ambition cannot be un-completed by later events.
A Throneworthy House may draw from the Throne deck, and may declare a Throne challenge once per round.
Epic length: 4 of 6 rather than 3 of 6.

throne.rule: A Throne challenge is declared by a Throneworthy House against the table.
The other House commits Military Levy against the challenger. Promises of type Forbearance come due here, and a Forbearance kept is a challenge unopposed.
The challenger commits Military Levy and may play Throne cards. The defender may play Combat cards.
The challenger must exceed the defender's total. Exceeding it wins the game.
Failing costs the challenger 3 Military Standing and gives the other House 2 Grievance, and they may not challenge again next round.
A challenger may instead pay the Throne's price: 12 Gold Standing and 8 Capital Standing, which no House will ever quite have, and which exists so that Goldwyn has a road nobody else has.

game.invention:
The trust ledger needs three. With two Houses there is no third party to exploit, no audience to remember, and breaking a promise at the moment it decides something is simply correct. A duel played on these rules without a fix is a payoff matrix with art on it.
The fix is to give the duel its third party: the Court, which is not a player and does not take turns, but which votes, remembers, and can be bought. Promises in a two-player game are sworn publicly before the Court, the Court's Favour rises with oaths kept and falls with oaths broken, and the Court holds the deciding vote. Betrayal now costs something again, because the party that remembers is still at the table.
At three and four Houses the Court is not used. The other Houses are the Court.

neutral_court.rule: The Court is a deck of 30 cards and a Favour track running -10 to +10 for each House, starting at 0.
All Promises are sworn before the Court. Keeping one gives +1 Favour only if it carried consideration; breaking one gives -2, and breaking one that carried consideration gives -3.

A promise that cost the promiser nothing does not impress the Court. It still binds, it is still recorded, and breaking it is still punished — but the Court is not moved by a man who promises what is free to promise. Measured: without this, and with the crown at +5, Favour won 72% of games and they lasted 7.8 rounds.

The Court holds one vote at every Council and casts it for the House with the higher Favour, abstaining below +3. It abstains below +3 because Favour starts at nothing and a single purchase would otherwise sell the Council for three Gold.
Favour may be bought at 3 Gold Levy per point, once per round, to a maximum of +3 by purchase. The five points above that cannot be bought, only earned.
At the end of each round the Court turns one card, which acts on the realm without preference.

At Favour +8 the Court crowns that House and the game ends. This is a road a House can walk while losing every fight, and +8 rather than +5 is what makes it a road: five kept promises is a shortcut, and with the crown at +5 it was taken in three games out of four. At +8, and with only paid promises counting, the four roads run 10% by force, 39% by the Court, 36% by outlasting and 15% by the round cap, over 17.2 rounds.
Bonds run between a House and a Minor Lord. There is no Bond between the two Houses; an opponent cannot be bound, only beaten, bought or outlasted.
Instigators may target the Court, moving the other House's Favour by -1.

death.rule: A House is dead when all three Standings reach 0, or when a card kills it.
A House at 0 in all three has FALLEN, not ended. Its claim outlives it.
A fallen House draws from the Ghost deck, may haunt once per round, does not vote -- its lords serve nobody -- and cannot win.

A fallen House may be restored, returning at 1 Standing in each resource with its Promise piles intact. What you did is not forgotten by dying. A card that returns it better than that is a card doing better than the general rule, which is what a card is for.
The Court decides whether a claim is heard at all: a fallen House is restored only while its Favour exceeds the living House's.
Drive your own Favour to the crown value while a House is fallen and its claim is EXTINGUISHED. That is the second death, and the one that ends the game.
death.note: Answering Q10, 2026-09-20. The decks are dealt. The reasoning was that if the dead can return, survivability changes, so a return needs a counter -- and the pool had none: of 1,066 cards exactly three touch a ghost's finality and two of them are drawn by the dead player, while the Ghost deck holds "draw from the Resurrection deck" and 26 of those 29 return the pretender at full strength, several of them better placed than they died. Ghosts as the pool shipped them made killing a rival a mistake. The counter is the Court, because the Court is already the organ that says who is legitimate: it "casts one vote, for the House with the higher Favour". A pretender is not banished, it is outbid for recognition -- and Favour is capped at +3 by purchase, so finishing a rival for good costs a campaign at Court and not a coin. Measured: The Last House fell from 33% of wins to 10%; killing a House stopped being a way to win and became a way to stop one winning.

condition.name: Claim by Force
condition.step: Exceed the other House's committed Military.

condition.name: The Purchased Throne
condition.step: Be Throneworthy and hold 7 Gold and 3 Capital Standing.
condition.note: Repriced 2026-09-20, from 12 Gold and 8 Capital. Those numbers came from the four-player board game's economy and made this road impossible rather than hard: it had never once been walked in any soak. Standing in this game mostly goes DOWN -- it is what a lost combat takes -- and measured over 300 games Goldwyn's TOTAL Standing across all three resources averages 4.2 and peaks at 11, against a road asking 20 between two of them. Seven is the point found by sweep where the road becomes GOLDWYN'S: below it Ravenmark takes it more often, because Ravenmark accumulates Gold as combat spoils, and above eight only Ravenmark can reach it at all. It now takes about 5% of games.

condition.name: The Golden Throne
condition.step: Hold 12 Gold Standing, and play the card that claims it.
condition.result: You win. No Throneworthy gate and no Capital: this is the one road that is purely Gold, which is what makes it Goldwyn's.
condition.note: Added 2026-09-20 and currently almost unreachable, which is recorded rather than hidden. Only 2 cards in 1,037 raise Gold Standing at all, so above Goldwyn's opening 8 the threshold cannot be grown into, and at 8 it would be a turn-one win. A hoarding victory needs a hoard and this design has none: Levy resets every turn and Standing decays. It wants a treasury -- somewhere unspent Gold accumulates -- which would also give the 47% of Levy that currently goes unspent somewhere to go. That is a mechanic and not a threshold, and it has not been built.

condition.name: The Last House
condition.step: The other House has fallen, and its claim has been extinguished: your Favour reached the crown while it was down.
condition.note: Changed 2026-09-20. Reducing a House to nothing is no longer the win; extinguishing its claim at Court is. Measured, the road fell from 33% of games to 10%, which is the intended shape: killing a House stopped being a way to win and became a way to stop one winning while you go and win properly.

condition.name: The Final King
condition.step: The round cap is reached, or a Cataclysm ends the realm.
Highest Total Power in Standing, ties broken by fewest Broken Words.

Pays 1 less for War deck access

Spying always fails

strengths.strength: +5 Gold Standing at start
+2 Gold Levy every turn beyond Standing

The Purchased Throne is a road only it can realistically walk

houses.note: The four below were added 2026-09-20. The first four each own a RESOURCE; these own a SUBSYSTEM, because four of them were built and idle. Measured over 200 games before these existed: lords held per House 0.08, Promises made 1.69 a game, Grievance 0.80 of a maximum ten. A system with no House that needs it does not get used, and a House is the cheapest way to make one matter. Eight Houses still means two chairs -- what changes is how much of the game you have not seen.

decks.note: 1,035 carried from Game of Treasons plus 160 new: the Promise, Lever, Court and Minor Lords decks, none of which had a parent. Removing the board cuts 64 of the carried cards — 17 naming movement, 36 naming castles or sieges, 11 naming the gauntlet — so the pool that actually converts is 971, and the manifest above is what it is being converted towards.
decks.cut: 57 pool cards are formally cut and will not be written. They are not a backlog; each wants something this design does not have, and most of them were already cut in principle by the line above. THE GAUNTLET. Every GAU card -- The Locked Gate, The Guardian, The Riddle, The Trial, The Execution, The Coronation, The Throne -- is a space on the parent game's road to the Throne. The note above already cuts the gauntlet with the board; they sat in the Ambition deck because that is where the pool filed them, and they are not Ambitions. Claim by Force replaced that road. The Ambition deck's real shortfall is therefore 20 genuine Ambitions still to write, not these. Win conditions not adopted: "Winner takes all; loser is eliminated", "Win if all living players vote for you", and the wagers. Offered 2026-09-20 and only the Gold road was taken. A card-in-play zone to steal or cancel a NAMED card already on the table. Cancelling the next card played needs no such zone and was built; reaching into one does. Table talk, messages and dice. There is no chat channel in the rules and nothing rolls that a card could reroll. Retreat, initiative and armour, from a game with a board. Combat here is one blind commit; what a retreat BOUGHT was converted instead, as OP_NO_SPOIL. The Lord Paramount as a seat rather than an office -- "decides your fate", "issues a decree". Here it is a title the Council elects, with a tax attached, and it makes no decisions of its own. A genuine third House: redirecting an attack to someone else, two players sharing the Paramountcy. Effects with three clauses. A Card holds two, and gen-cards.py refuses a third rather than dropping it quietly.
decks.cut_note: The deck targets are NOT reduced by the cut, and that is deliberate. A pool card that cannot convert does not shrink the deck it would have gone into; the deck still wants that many cards and they now have to be written rather than converted. The Ambition deck is the clearest case: 27 of the cut are gauntlet cards the pool filed under Ambition, they were never part of the 30 Ambitions this design wants, and reducing the target to 3 because of them would have been a lie. What the cut changes is the MEANING of the shortfall, which extract-cards.py now reports separately: the pool is spent, so what remains is new writing and not a conversion backlog. The figure was also simply wrong until today -- it read 348, of which 186 was an accounting fault, sub-decks counted apart from the parents they fold into.

card_schema.field: Play on turn, Instant, Reaction, Permanent, Lever, Ambition, Promise, Minor Lord, Resolve on draw.
Levy paid to play, as "2G", "1M 1C", "3C 2Grv", or "0". M Military, C Capital, G Gold, Grv Grievance. A cost in Standing is written "2G!" with the bang meaning permanent.
Core, Growth, Combat, Bond, Promise, Reputation, Council, Chaos.
One line, imperative, written so a classifier can read a delta, a target and a duration out of it.
Names the public state the card inspects, if any: broken_words, word_kept, grievance, unrest, standing, throneworthy, favour.
card_schema.writing_rule: Effects name Levy or Standing explicitly. "+2 Military" alone is ambiguous and is not acceptable in this design; the parent game's classifier could not tell them apart and it cost a fortnight.
A card that cannot be carried out in the current state is inert. The AI plays an inert card only when it has no other, and the count of inert plays is printed at the end of every game.

cards.note: What follows is a seed, not the full 1,135. It fixes the vocabulary, the cost shapes and the categories, so that the remaining cards can be written — or converted from the parent pool — against a settled pattern rather than inventing one per card. Every mechanic in this document appears in at least one card below; if a system has no card, it does not exist.

AS OF 2026-09-20 THIS SECTION IS NO LONGER THE CARD TABLE. The conversion happened, and it happened in CARDS.tsv: 1,037 cards live, 1,003 of the pool's 1,066. The 157 below are still the seed. Two consequences worth knowing before editing this file. First, CARDS.tsv is no longer generated from here — the Makefile rule was removed, because with it live, editing the authority to record a decision made it newer than CARDS.tsv and the next build silently rebuilt the live set from a sixth of it. extract-cards.py now refuses to shrink a table it did not fill. Second, this section and CARDS.tsv can disagree, and where they do the rules above still win and the card table is what is played. Folding all 1,037 back in here, so this is generated again and the two cannot drift, is outstanding work.

networking.status: all three, and two of them are one implementation
networking.note:
All three are wanted, so all three are built. The thing that makes that affordable is that they are not three programs: a central server and a trusted host are the same authority binary run by different people, and the difference between them is who is trusted and what the interface says about it. Only commit-reveal is a separate mechanism, and it is a layer over the same protocol rather than a replacement for it.
What made this cheap was written down before it was needed. The engine is a pure function from state and action to state; every change goes through court_apply; and court_view already hands a seat exactly what it is entitled to see and nothing else, which is requirement N1 satisfied by construction rather than by filtering. A Seat is five function pointers, so a remote seat is five functions that write an Action and wait for a View.
networking.requirement: There is exactly one authority for hidden state, and no client ever receives hidden state it is not entitled to see. Filtering it in the client is not an implementation of this requirement.
The random stream is owned by the authority and is seeded. A client cannot draw its own cards.
Simultaneous decisions — commitment in combat, keep-or-break at Reckoning — are collected from both seats before either is revealed to either seat.
Every state change is a described action, validated by the authority. A client proposes; it never asserts.

A disconnected or timed-out seat is played by the machine from what that seat legitimately knows, and the game does not stall. A seat that goes quiet at Reckoning keeps its promises by default, because defaulting to betrayal would make disconnection a strategy.

A server holds many people at once. They arrive, give a name, see who else is there, talk to all of them, and start a game with one of them -- and when that game ends they are back where they started. The client is the only way any of this is done.
This replaces the shape the server had, which was written down as a virtue and was really a limitation: "there is no lobby and no matchmaking, only the next person to connect." That is honest for a duel arranged beforehand by two people who already know each other. It is useless for a room.
What it costs is the accept loop. Fork-per-game works because a game is two sockets and no shared state; a lobby is shared state by definition -- who is here, what they said, which tables are open -- so it cannot be forked, and the parent has to hold every connection at once and multiplex them. That is net_wait again, with the listener in the set.
A game is still forked. The lobby hands two channels to a child and forgets them; the child is the authority for that game and nothing about N1 changes. When the child exits the sockets close, and the client returns to the lobby on its own.
Names are not identity. There are no passwords, nothing is reserved, and two people may pick the same name -- this is a LAN game and the interface should not imply otherwise. Authentication is a separate thing and is not built.

A game between two people carries talk between them. This is a game about promises, and a promise made only in the formal language of the Promise deck is a thinner thing than one argued for first; the chat is part of the play, not an amenity beside it.
It relays through the authority rather than between the clients: there is already exactly one machine both seats are connected to, a second connection between them would be a second thing to firewall, and a peer link would let one client learn the other's address. The authority relays the text and does not read it.
Two constraints the obvious implementation fails. First, the line arrives when the sender chooses, not when they are asked -- so the authority cannot only ever read a channel while waiting for that seat's answer, or a player's talk would sit unseen until their turn came round. Second, talk is not an action: it is never validated, never enters the Game, and never reaches court_apply. It is the one thing on this wire that the engine does not see.

protocol.rule: One wire format for all three: a client sends an Action, the authority replies with that seat's View. Both are plain data — an Action is seven small integers and a View has no pointers — so the format is mechanical and a client may be written in any language.
The same protocol runs over a pipe for a local game, a socket for a host or a server, and a pair of sockets under commit-reveal. The transport is the only thing that changes.
The authority never sends a Game. It sends a View, per seat, built by court_view.

networking.state:
Built: a server that seats one person against the machine or two people against each other, over the same protocol, forking per game. court_serve_n takes a channel per seat and a null is the machine, so the loop does not know which kind of game it is playing.
A client that wants a person says so on joining and one that says nothing gets the machine, so every client written before pairing existed still works. Only two clients that both asked for a person are paired.
The seat that is not being asked is sent its own View, so a player can watch the table move rather than staring at a frozen board until their go comes round. It is built by court_view for that seat, so N1 is not weakened by saying it more often.
Not built: commit-reveal, which the option below says to build last; and any authentication, so this is a LAN game.

option.name: Central server
option.satisfies: N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 directly. The server is the referee and the hidden state never leaves it.
option.costs: Hosting, an account system, availability. The game stops working when you stop paying for it.

option.name: Trusted host
option.satisfies: N2 N3 N4 by construction, and N1 only as far as the host is trusted: the hosting player's machine holds the other seat's hidden Bonds and Ambitions.
option.costs: Free to run, and unsound against anyone willing to read their own memory.
option.rule: The interface says so. A client connected to a trusted host displays it, at the join and on the table, and never quietly assumes it. A player who does not mind is entitled to not mind; a player who has not been told is not.
option.note: The same binary as the central server, run by a player instead of by you.

option.name: Peer to peer with commitments
option.satisfies: All five without a server, at the cost of real work.
option.mechanism: Every simultaneous choice is published as a salted hash and revealed afterwards; a mismatch forfeits. Every hidden counter is held by its owner as a running commitment, so a Revolution count cannot be edited retroactively, only revealed and checked. Shuffles are produced by combined seeds contributed by both seats, so neither chooses the deck order alone.
option.costs: Commit-reveal on nearly every phase, a verification path for every hidden track, and a forfeit rule that has to be right or it becomes the exploit.
option.note: Built last, because it is the only one that is a new mechanism rather than a new address, and because the other two will have shaken the protocol out first. It is also the only one that makes betrayal provable rather than merely alleged, which suits the subject.

networking.open_question: Asynchronous play, where a round may take a day, changes N5 from a disconnection policy into the main mode of play. Still undecided, and it still constrains the answer: an asynchronous game needs the authority to outlive both clients, which the trusted host cannot do and commit-reveal can only do by storing commitments somewhere.

engine_contract.note: Carried from treasons-c, where each of these was learned rather than assumed.
engine_contract.rule: Headless from the first commit. A game that cannot be played ten thousand times without a screen is a game that cannot be measured.
A seed replays a game exactly, including every AI decision.
Invariants are armed in testing and assert the rules as the game runs. A log line beginning INV is a bug and never a quirk.
Generated card tables are declared build dependencies, so that a table cannot be regenerated without relinking the binary that reads it.
Any change is judged by paired build: the previous commit and the new one, over the same three ranges of seeds, never one.
State and action in, state out. No hidden mutation, because the networking decision above depends on it and has not been made.
engine_contract.measure: The share of played cards that changed nothing. In the parent game this was 53% and it is the single most honest number the engine produces.
Should sit near 1 in 10. Near zero means promises are priced from where the liar stands. Near half means they are priced by what they would buy and nothing is holding them.
Must not sit pinned at 10. That was the parent game's standing defect and the sinks above exist to fix it.
Across a few hundred games, no House should win more than about a third more often than the worst.
If Houses routinely end turns with Levy in hand, the costs are too low and there is no curve.

conversion.note: 1,035 cards exist in design.xml. They do not need rewriting, but they do need three mechanical passes, and the third is the only one that needs judgement.
conversion.pass: 64 cards are cut, not converted: 17 name movement or spaces, 36 name castles or sieges, and 11 name the gauntlet or the rings. The figure of 19 that this design first carried counted only movement, and the ancestry note removes castles and sieges as well. The real price of removing the board is 6.2% of the pool, not under 2%.

Every effect reading "+2 Military" must become "+2 Military Levy" or "+2 Military Standing permanently". This is mechanical for most cards and is the pass that must not be skipped: the parent classifier could not tell the two apart because the design never distinguished them.

Every card needs a cost, which the parent pool has none of. A first pass can be generated from the size of the effect and then tuned by soak, but it is the pass that decides whether the game has a curve.
Cards that inspect public state get a reads attribute. Most will have none; the Reputation category is where the new game lives and it should grow well beyond the seed above.

The parent's type attribute is mostly the name of the deck a card sits in, and it carries 36 categories against the 8 in card_schema. Neither maps itself. This pass was not in the original list and is purely mechanical.
conversion.measured: Running passes 1, 2, 4 and 5 over the parent pool converts 942 cards and leaves 930 of the merged 1,066 effects unreadable by the classifier, collapsing to 517 distinct shapes of which 353 appear exactly once. There is no small set of patterns that unlocks the pool. Pass 2 is therefore not mechanical: these cards need their effects rewritten onto the opcodes this engine already has, rather than parsed in the vocabulary they arrived in. That is the largest single piece of work remaining.
conversion.extractor_note: extract-cards.py reads this file almost unchanged. Its board block must be deleted, and it must carry the new cost and reads attributes through to CARDS.tsv. Its deck-count check works as written, and unlike the parent design the total here is arithmetic that closes.

open_questions.settled: Whether the tax takes Standing or Levy. It takes Levy. Measured over three ranges of 300 seeds: Standing gave a 14.6x win spread and handed whoever led first 54% of games; Levy gave 1.55x and 21-26%.

What the Court is impressed by, and what crowns. Only promises that carried consideration, and +8. Both came from the soak: as first written the Court crowned in 72% of games after 7.8 rounds, which is not a third road but the only one.
Whether a two-player game uses Ambitions. It does; they are the road to the Throne and the only hidden thing a Disclosure promise can trade.
open_questions.question: Networking, below. Asynchronous play should be settled first. Two seats make a trusted host far more tempting and no more sound.
Whether the 6 Ambitions come from a shared deck or one per House. Shared makes them contested, which at two players is sharper than it was at four.
Whether a House may hold more than one Promise with the other at once. At two players this is no longer a question about legibility but about whether the whole game can be one negotiation.
Whether Broken Words should ever be cleared. Vipren's Nothing Was Agreed launders one, once. With the Court reading the piles this matters more than it did.
Starting hand size and opening draw, which cannot be chosen except by soak.
Whether the Lord Paramount should exist at all now that it is elected rather than accrued. It gives the Council something to decide; it is also still the mechanic that ends games earliest.
How many Minor Lords may be in play at once, and whether an unbound lord sits in a neutral row both Houses can reach or is played straight into a House.
open_questions.answered: Whether the Ghost and Resurrection decks are dealt at all in the standard game, given death ends it. ANSWERED: they are dealt, and death no longer ends it. See <death>.
